_readme: Finance role taxonomy used by intel/taxonomy.py. Patterns are case-insensitive regex fragments. The loader wraps every fragment in word boundaries, turns ' ?' into optional separators and ' ' into one-or-more separators (space, hyphen, slash), so write 'sales (and|&) trading' rather than escaping. Signals: title hits weigh 4, department hits 2, description hits 1 each (distinct patterns, capped per category). company_priors add points when the employer type makes a category more likely, but only when the posting already carries a finance signal or a generic finance title word. associate_stage decides whether an untitled 'Associate' is entry-level (post-undergrad) or experienced (post-MBA / post-banking) in that category. Each job family is a board: track names the boards it shares employer types, skills and resume vocabulary with (see tracks), occupation_beats_finance lets a technical occupation in its titles beat finance words, skill_groups are the skill groups Settings and onboarding show for it and employer_types the employers a resume aimed at it proposes (a specialty's own come first). Job families (non_finance_families) are matched on the title in order; software, data_ml, hardware, healthcare, product and design carry specialties (subcategories) scored the same way, where title words before the first comma or dash count most, tie_priority settles ties, related specialties earn partial credit for each other, also_targets lets a specialty target count a finance group or another board's specialty as a match, and company_priors may name specialties (software.game_dev) but never make a role finance. fallback_title is a board's second tier: words that place a title only when Finance and every board's title words left it in 'other'. claims are named rules by which a board takes a title another board or Finance places (see its _readme), and stage_rules a board's own career levels. test_posting_titles are titles an employer gives its test requisitions ('DO NOT APPLY - TEST REQ'): such a posting is no opening, so it leaves every board the way a passed deadline does. pay_rate_phrases are pay lines in a title ('Enhanced Pay Rates', '(**New Rates**)'): finance title words are read without them, so such a 'Rates' doesn't make a CT technologist a Fixed Income role. function_title names a control function a finance group is (Operational Risk: compliance): a finance title naming it is placed there whatever desk or product it covers and whatever the posting's prose adds ('Compliance Officer - Equities' is compliance work, not Equities), unless function_unless words name other work ('Tax Compliance' stays Accounting); a title another filter of that group takes keeps it ('Compliance Model Governance' stays Model Risk).

non_finance_families._order: Checked in this order; first title match wins. Clinical roles take precedence over generic analytics; AI & data precedes software. fallback_title words are read only after the finance decision and every board's title words, for titles still in 'other'. domain_title patterns name a subject (cybersecurity, ML) rather than an occupation, so they only decide the family when the title names no business occupation (product manager, counsel, recruiter, sales).

claims._readme: Named rules by which this board takes a title that another board, or Finance, places today (plans/healthcare-board.md, D1 and D2). from lists where the title may be placed ('finance', a board, 'other'); title must match and unless must not. With subject, employer_types or description, the posting also needs a subject in the title, an employer of one of those types, or min_description distinct description phrases; a finance title keeps Finance when its description reads as finance in two phrases or more, unless the title names the subject. sole_occupation: not when the title also names a tech or business occupation ('Nurse Recruiter'). subcategory names the filter.

program_windows._readme: Yearly windows of this board's training programs, shown in Calendar to profiles with the board (D16). The dates are typical: each program sets its own. 'filters' and 'licences' narrow a window to profiles that chose one of those filters or hold or expect one of those licences; a profile with neither sees every window. 'after_graduation' dates a window from the profile's graduation month instead.

stage_rules._readme: Product's own career levels (plans/product-design-board.md 5.4, D17 to D21), read like Healthcare's: before the shared ones, only for this board's postings, the first level whose title matches and whose unless doesn't wins. A bare product, program or project manager is Experienced, not Senior (the shared rules read 'manager' as a level); Associate PM and PM I are Entry; APM and rotational programs, apprenticeships and dated titles are New grad; a bank's 'Product Manager, Associate' and Capital One's 'Principal Associate' are Experienced. An MBA internship is the shared Summer Associate level (it sets post_mba); a team word before 'program manager' ('Internship Program Manager') names the programs the job runs, not its level. Principal, Director and Head / Chief change only the label. new_grad_program is Healthcare's key, so APM programs and apprenticeships show its NEW GRAD PROGRAM badge.

tracks._readme: A track is the boards that share employer types, skills and resume vocabulary. A board names its track in non_finance_families (Finance's is "finance"); a company type names its tracks in companies.json and a skill its track in skills.json. label and employer_heading name the track in Settings, where its employer types are shown to its boards; employer_noun ends the Why line of a company on the track ("Big Tech — recognized tech employer") for a profile with one of its boards. skills_from lists the boards ("other" for postings no board places) whose postings read the track's skills; Finance postings never do. resume opens the track for a resume whose degree matches degree (a regular expression, case-insensitive) or with a job or project title placed on one of its boards; signals are [target role, weight, regular expression] in the order they are read, each distinct phrase counting once per resume block.
